pedagogy.summary: Fluency within 1000 is NOT just 'do columnar faster' — it is the flexible, adaptive choice of the most efficient method for THESE particular numbers (Threlfall; NCETM 'intelligent practice'). The child should have three tools in play — the standard columnar algorithm, mental strategies (compensation, near-doubles, place-value partitioning), and counting up on an empty number line for close subtractions — and pick well. Efficiency and the add/sub inverse relationship (checking) are the goals, not a single rote procedure.
bestPractices: Contrast strategies explicitly: put the same problem up and ask 'clever way vs plod way?' — build adaptive expertise rather than defaulting to the algorithm
Use counting-up on an empty number line for close subtractions (300-298, 401-399) so difference-as-distance is felt
Teach compensation for near-multiples (525+199 = 525+200-1) alongside the algorithm
Always link subtraction to addition for checking (inverse), not re-counting
Reserve the standard columnar algorithm for problems where no shortcut helps (456+287)
keyRepresentations: Place-value columns / base-ten exchange (the algorithm's meaning)
Empty number line (counting up for difference)
Hundred square / place-value chart for +/-10, +/-100 jumps
commonMisconceptions: Reaches for the column algorithm for every problem even when counting up or compensating is far quicker (strategy inflexibility)
Smaller-from-larger subtraction bug — subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in a column regardless of position
Cannot decompose to subtract when a column is zero (borrow-across-zero)
Treats subtraction as unrelated to addition — re-counts to check instead of using the inverse

learn.summary: Fluency within 1000 is adaptive strategy choice, not just faster column arithmetic: pupils match the most efficient method to the particular numbers. The child should hold three tools and pick well — the standard columnar algorithm (for problems where no shortcut helps, e.g. 456+287), mental strategies (compensation 525+199 = 525+200-1, near-doubles, place-value partitioning), and counting up on an empty number line for close subtractions (300-298, 401-399). Subtraction is linked to addition for checking (inverse), not re-counting. Learners also need to handle known systematic subtraction bugs: smaller-from-larger, and borrow/decompose across a zero.

activities.title: Two-track strategy bench: match the method to the numbers
feedback: If the child reaches for columns on 300-298: put the two numbers on an empty number line and ask 'how far apart are they?'; contrast the steps each method took. Build the habit of glancing at the numbers before choosing.
If the child uses the algorithm well on 456+287: affirm that this is exactly where the column method earns its place.
When checking, if the child re-does the subtraction: prompt them to add the answer back using the item's own numbers — for 300-298, does 2 + 298 return 300? — to make the inverse-check routine.
activities.rationale: Running two tracks side by side lets the child feel the cost of a poor method choice and the payoff of a good one; reversing with 456+287 keeps the algorithm valued rather than discarded. A live recomputing bench with a visible timer is one concrete way to make the cost of the choice visible; a paper version (solve both ways, compare, time with a clock) can serve the same purpose.
sourceClaims: The defining standard for fluency within 1000 is strategic, not rote: pupils 'fluently add and subtract within 1000 using strategies and algorithms based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction' — a range of algorithms may be used.

Adaptive expertise — choosing a strategy suited to the specific numbers (e.g. counting up for close subtractions, compensation for near-multiples) — is a distinct, teachable goal beyond executing the standard algorithm.
learnerActions: Meet a problem such as 300-298. Before computing, glance at the numbers and predict which method will be quickest.
Solve it two ways side by side: an empty-number-line track (count up from 298 to 300) and a column-algorithm track (set up and exchange across the zero). Time or step-count both.
Compare: on 300-298 the number line jumps the gap in one hop of 2 while the column track is still exchanging across the zero (and may trip over it).
Now try 456+287 the same way and compare: no obvious shortcut stands out for these numbers, so the column algorithm is a sensible, efficient choice here.

Add a check step using the inverse, with this activity's own numbers: for 300-298, add your answer (2) back to 298 and confirm you reach 300; for 456+287 (=743), subtract one addend from the total to recover the other.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency means matching the method to the numbers, not grinding one algorithm; close numbers favour counting up, near-multiples favour compensation, and messy numbers favour the column algorithm.

activities.title: Sort first, then solve: which method would you choose?
feedback: If a problem is mis-sorted, ask the child to say how far apart the numbers are, or how close one is to a round number, then re-sort.
If the child sorts correctly but reverts to one method when computing, point back to their own sort and ask them to honour the chosen method.
For 502-5, if the child tries to count up the whole gap or reaches for column borrowing, point out that only 5 is subtracted, so counting back 5 or compensating is far quicker.
activities.rationale: A categorise-then-compute task drills adaptive selection explicitly and makes the selection step visible. Sorting and justifying is recognition-plus-reasoning; it checks classification but does not itself elicit the computation, so pair it with actual calculation so selection is tested against real arithmetic.
sourceClaims: Adaptive expertise — choosing a strategy suited to the specific numbers (e.g. counting up for close subtractions, compensation for near-multiples) — is a distinct, teachable goal beyond executing the standard algorithm.
learnerActions: Sort 8 problems into three piles: 'count up' (close numbers), 'compensate' (near a multiple like +199), and 'column' (no shortcut helps).
For each problem, state in one phrase why it belongs in that pile ('these two are close, so I count up').

Transfer: given a new pair such as 502-5, decide which method is quickest — note the two numbers are far apart but only 5 is taken away, so counting back 5 or compensation beats a column borrow across the zero.
activities.intendedInsight: Strategy selection is a distinct, assessable skill: you can name and justify why a particular method fits particular numbers before doing any arithmetic.

activities.title: Fix the subtraction bugs: smaller-from-larger and borrow across zero
feedback: If the child writes 265 (smaller digit taken from larger in the ones and tens): return to concrete base-ten exchange on the failing columns, showing that 8 cannot be taken from 3 and 6 cannot be taken from 0 without exchanging, and that the hundreds must then drop from 7 to 6.
If the child stalls at the zero, writes 0 in the tens, or borrows incorrectly: model exchanging one hundred into ten tens first (703 = 6 hundreds, 9 tens, 13 ones) with blocks before the digits.
Finish with the inverse check: add the answer (135) back to 568 and confirm you reach 703.
activities.rationale: Smaller-from-larger and borrow-from-zero are documented, stable subtraction bugs, so targeted concrete exchange work on the exact failing column addresses a known error source rather than a one-off slip.
sourceClaims: Smaller-from-larger and borrow-from-zero are systematic, documented, STABLE subtraction bugs: borrow-from-zero (change a 0 to 9 but fail to keep borrowing left) is the single most common bug in Brown & Burton's data (107/1325); smaller-from-larger was used by 54; ~40% of students showed consistently buggy behaviour.
learnerActions: Work 703-568 with base-ten materials (or place-value chips) before writing digits: exchange one hundred into ten tens, then one ten into ten ones, so 703 becomes 6 hundreds, 9 tens, 13 ones.
Check each column: confirm you cannot take 8 from 3 in the ones without exchanging — you do not simply subtract the smaller digit from the larger.
Complete the written algorithm, keeping the borrow moving left across the zero (the answer is 135).

Compare your answer with a wrong answer like 265 and explain which columns were mishandled (265 comes from taking the smaller digit from the larger in each column: the ones (3 take 8) and tens (0 take 6) skipped their exchanges, so the hundreds was never reduced from 7 to 6; the ones digit 5 matches the correct answer only by coincidence).
activities.intendedInsight: Column subtraction requires exchanging by place value; a top digit smaller than the bottom digit means you must decompose, and when a zero column must give to the column on its right (as in 703-568), it first needs an exchange from the hundreds — not leaving the column as 0.

activities.title: Strategy-menu reference and 'convince me' justification
feedback: If the child cannot justify a choice beyond 'that's how you do it', ask them to compare the number of steps their method took with an alternative.
Use the menu wall as a reference, not a crutch: encourage the child to predict the pick before consulting it.
activities.rationale: A static menu offers a useful reference but cannot by itself let the child experience the cost of a choice; a justification exchange surfaces reasoning. Both support, rather than replace, actually doing and comparing the methods in the bench activity.
sourceClaims: Adaptive expertise — choosing a strategy suited to the specific numbers (e.g. counting up for close subtractions, compensation for near-multiples) — is a distinct, teachable goal beyond executing the standard algorithm.
learnerActions: Build or use a strategy-menu wall with three worked examples, one per method (count up, compensate, column), each labelled with when it is the smart pick.
After solving a problem, explain to a partner or coach why your chosen method was quickest for those numbers.
Respond to a challenge ('convince me your method was quickest') by pointing to the number features that made your choice efficient.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to articulate why a method fits particular numbers consolidates adaptive expertise and exposes whether a choice was reasoned or habitual.

constraints: The goal is efficient, adaptive method choice plus the add/sub inverse for checking — not speed at a single rote procedure.
A static strategy-menu poster is a reference only: it cannot let the child experience the choice or feel its cost, so pair it with activities that involve actually doing and comparing methods.
A sort/categorise step checks selection reasoning but should be paired with real computation so pupils also execute the chosen method correctly.
A justification dialogue surfaces reasoning but does not replace actually doing and comparing the methods; keep real computation central.
Subtraction checking should use addition (inverse), not re-counting the subtraction, and each check should use the numbers of the problem actually solved.
Reserve the standard column algorithm for problems where no shortcut helps (e.g. 456+287); do not treat it as the default for every problem.
Base-ten cutouts/blocks are concrete approximations of place-value structure; use the exchange physically before the written digits for borrow-across-zero.
Computation within 1000 is planar place-value work; the proposed number-line and column representations are sufficient here — a third spatial dimension is not required for this topic.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched this session. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The source marks the Threlfall/NCETM 'intelligent practice' claim as not fetched this session (verified:false); treat the adaptive-expertise principle as plausibly supported but unverified here.

Worked arithmetic check: 300-298 = 2 (one hop of 2 by counting up); 525+199 = 525+200-1 = 724; 456+287 = 743; 703-568 = 135 (703 = 6 hundreds, 9 tens, 13 ones; the buggy 265 arises from smaller-from-larger/flip errors). These arithmetic facts were verified during this rewrite; no source effectiveness claims were verified.

The original 'only a live 2D bench can let the child pick a method and FEEL the cost', 'dialogue cannot provide', and '3D adds nothing' claims were softened to narrowly-scoped affordances with limits; the comparative-necessity wording is not established by the cited sources. Stopwatch timing is likewise one concrete scaffold, not a requirement.

502-5 is used as a transfer item; it is a 'small takeaway from a round-ish number' where counting back or compensation is quick, NOT a close-numbers/difference-as-distance case. The original gap note's 'these are close' phrasing is loose; confirm the intended discriminating feature when authoring.

Inverse checks are scoped to each activity's own problem numbers: the 300-298/456+287 bench uses its own numbers, and the 703-568 inverse check (135+568=703) sits in the subtraction-bug activity where that problem is actually worked.

probeDeeper: Which of those four was quickest for you, and why?
Could you have done 456 + 287 a cleverer way, or was the column method best there?
What about 502 - 5 - column method, or something quicker?
Show me how you'd check the 703 - 568 answer without redoing the subtraction.
assess.correctAnswer: Flexible and fluent: solves 300-298 by counting up / difference of 2 (not columnar borrowing), adds 199 by 525+200-1 (compensation), uses the columnar algorithm for 456+287 where no shortcut helps, and handles 703-568 with a correct exchange across the zero. Justifies each choice by the numbers ('these two are close, so I counted up').

errorPatterns.pattern: Sets up 300-298 in columns and grinds a borrow-across-zero instead of noticing the two numbers are almost the same ('you just do the column method for take-aways')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Put the two numbers on an empty number line and ask 'how far apart are they?'; contrast the time each method took. Build the habit of glancing at the numbers before choosing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reaches for the algorithm on 300-298 and 525+199 and never counts up or compensates, even when prompted to find a quicker way

errorPatterns.pattern: In 703-568 subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in each column regardless of which is on top (smaller-from-larger bug)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to concrete base-ten exchange on the specific failing column; show that you cannot take 8 from 3 without exchanging.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Writes an answer like 265; the tens/ones are 'flipped' where the top digit is smaller

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot decompose to subtract in 703-568 because the tens column is 0 (borrow-across-zero)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model exchanging one hundred into ten tens first (703 = 6 hundreds, 9 tens, 13 ones) with base-ten blocks before the digits.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Stalls at the zero, writes 0 in the tens, or borrows incorrectly

errorPatterns.pattern: Having answered, re-counts the subtraction to check instead of adding the answer back (inverse not linked)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, do not reteach: 'add your answer to 568 - do you get back to 703?' Make the inverse-check routine.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked to check, redoes the same subtraction rather than using addition

responseLevels.gap: Reaches for one method for all four (usually columnar), misapplies it on the near-numbers, and cannot say why that method was chosen.
responseLevels.full: Selects an efficient method per item and justifies it by the numbers, and checks via the inverse; transfers the 'are these close?' judgement to a new pair such as 502-5.
responseLevels.partial: Computes all four correctly but uses the same method throughout - can name a method but does not match it to the numbers, and cannot transfer the 'these are close' idea to 502-5.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put these four in front of the child one at a time and say: 'Solve each one however you think is best, and tell me why you chose that way.' 300 - 298; 525 + 199; 456 + 287; 703 - 568. Watch WHICH method they reach for each time and listen to the 'why'.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 300-298 and 525+199 punish a child who owns only one tool: a rote columnar solver laboriously borrows across the zero on 300-298 (and often errs), whereas a flexible child sees the difference is just 2. 456+287 conversely rewards the algorithm. The mix separates true fluency (right method for these numbers) from mere procedure.
